meta.title: Who originally recorded "Iko Iko"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a Dixie Cups original. It was first cut as “Jock-A-Mo” by James “Sugar Boy” Crawford and His Cane Cutters, Checker 787, November 1953.
meta.ogDescription: The Dixie Cups had the 1965 hit. The record came first in November 1953 as “Jock-A-Mo” by James “Sugar Boy” Crawford on Checker.

answer.label: Not a Dixie Cups original — a November 1953 James “Sugar Boy” Crawford and His Cane Cutters single called “Jock-A-Mo”
answer.originalArtist: James "Sugar Boy" Crawford and His Cane Cutters
answer.originalArtistDates: 1934-2012 · New Orleans rhythm & blues singer, songwriter and bandleader
answer.sourceLine: Most people meet this song through The Dixie Cups’ 1965 Red Bird single and assume the trio invented it. They did not: the record already existed, cut in New Orleans as “Jock-A-Mo” by James “Sugar Boy” Crawford and His Cane Cutters and issued on Chess’s Checker subsidiary as Checker 787 in November 1953. Crawford wrote it, setting phrases chanted by the Mardi Gras Indians to music. The single never reached the national charts, and by the time the retitled version was a hit the original was known mainly in New Orleans — which is why the 1965 record is so widely taken for the source.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.artist: James "Sugar Boy" Crawford and His Cane Cutters
original.label: Checker Records
original.released: Issued as a single on Checker Records, catalogue number 787, in November 1953, credited to Sugar Boy and His Cane Cutters, with “You, You, You” on the flip. It featured Dave Lastie on tenor saxophone. Some catalogues, including MusicBrainz ↗, date the release 1954.
original.charted: Did not chart. Wikipedia states plainly that the single did not make the charts; it circulated locally and was popular around the New Orleans Carnival season that followed.
original.cover: The Dixie Cups’ version, retitled “Iko Iko”, was released in March 1965 on Red Bird Records and peaked at No. 20 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 20 R&B and No. 23 in the UK. It grew out of an unplanned studio jam in New York with improvised percussion. The Belle Stars’ 1982 recording reached No. 35 in the UK and later No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 after its use in the 1988 film Rain Man.

trail: The Wikipedia article on the song ↗ states that James “Sugar Boy” Crawford and his Cane Cutters released it as “Jock-A-Mo” on Checker 787 in November 1953, and that the single did not make the charts.

The Internet Archive’s Great 78 Project ↗ holds a preservation transfer of the physical Checker 787 disc, credited to Sugar Boy and his Cane Cutters, composer Crawford — the object itself, not a reissue.
MusicBrainz ↗ catalogues the Checker 787 single “Jock-A-Mo” / “You, You, You” by Sugar Boy and His Cane Cutters, with the A-side recording running about 2:27.
Crawford’s own biography page ↗ records that Leonard Chess signed his band and renamed them Sugar Boy and his Cane Cutters, and that he authored the song The Dixie Cups later made a hit.

authors.name: James “Sugar Boy” Crawford
authors.heading: He wrote it and he cut it first
authors.bio: Crawford started on trombone and led a New Orleans band that Leonard Chess signed to Checker, renaming them Sugar Boy and his Cane Cutters. In November 1953 they recorded “Jock-A-Mo”, which Crawford built by setting phrases chanted by the Mardi Gras Indians to music. The record sold locally and never charted nationally. A severe beating by state troopers in 1963 incapacitated him for two years and effectively ended his commercial career; by 1969 he was singing only in church, and he lived to see the song become a standard, appearing on HBO’s Treme in the year he died.

authors.name: The Dixie Cups
authors.heading: The version everyone actually knows
authors.metaLine: New Orleans vocal trio · Red Bird Records · March 1965
authors.bio: Barbara Ann Hawkins, her sister Rosa Lee and their cousin Joan Marie Johnson were already stars from “Chapel of Love” when an unplanned jam in a New York studio — voices and improvised percussion rather than a band arrangement — was captured and released in March 1965 as “Iko Iko”. It reached No. 20 on the Hot 100, and on its own terms it is a wonderful record: sparse, hypnotic and nothing like a conventional 1965 pop single. The only error in the popular account is chronological.

misattribution.heading: Setting the record straight
misattribution.intro: The confusion here is unusually layered, because the song reached the public under different names in different decades.

items.why: Their Red Bird single is the version that charted, the version that got covered, and the version most listeners heard first — so it reads as the source.

items.who: Sugar Boy and His Cane Cutters, November 1953
items.why: Released as “Jock-A-Mo” on Checker 787 with “You, You, You” on the flip. It did not chart, which is exactly why the later title stuck.

Crawford wrote the 1953 song from Mardi Gras Indian chants. He sued after the 1965 hit; under the 1967 settlement Crawford made no claim to authorship or ownership of “Iko Iko” and was credited 25 per cent for US public performances, and a 2002 jury later affirmed The Dixie Cups as its writers against a rival claim by their former manager Joe Jones.

The British group’s recording reached No. 35 in the UK, then climbed to No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 after appearing in Rain Man in 1988 — introducing a whole audience to the song via a cover of a cover.

misattribution.truthLine: The Dixie Cups gave it its famous name and its hit record. James “Sugar Boy” Crawford gave it its first.

context.heading: Why the second version became the first one everyone knows
lead: A record that does not chart leaves almost no trace. “Jock-A-Mo” came out on Checker in November 1953, sold around New Orleans through the Carnival season, and stopped there. The gap that matters is as much geographic as chronological: outside Louisiana there was simply nothing to remember it by when a New York studio jam surfaced under a new title in March 1965.

The retitling did the rest. A listener who knows the song as “Iko Iko” has no reason to go looking for “Jock-A-Mo”, and The Dixie Cups’ arrangement — voices and improvised percussion, no band — sounds so unlike a produced 1953 R&B single that hearing both back to back does not obviously suggest one came from the other. Crawford thought otherwise, and the courts eventually split the difference: under the 1967 settlement Crawford made no claim to authorship or ownership of “Iko Iko” and was credited 25 per cent for US public performances, and The Dixie Cups’ authorship of their version survived a challenge as late as 2002.
detailsBody: Early 1950s — James “Sugar Boy” Crawford leads a New Orleans band; Leonard Chess signs them to Checker and renames them Sugar Boy and his Cane Cutters.
November 1953 — “Jock-A-Mo” is issued as Checker 787, backed with “You, You, You”, with Dave Lastie on tenor saxophone. It does not chart.
March 1965 — The Dixie Cups release the song as “Iko Iko” on Red Bird; it reaches No. 20 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 20 R&B and No. 23 in the UK.
1967 — Crawford’s suit is settled: he makes no claim to authorship or ownership of “Iko Iko” and is credited 25 per cent for US public performances.
1982, 1988 and 1989 — The Belle Stars reach No. 35 in the UK; the song appears in Rain Man in 1988; the re-release reaches No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 in March 1989.
2002 — A jury rejects a claim by The Dixie Cups’ former manager Joe Jones and affirms the trio as the writers of “Iko Iko”.
context.pull: It did not chart, and then it changed its name. Either alone would have been enough.

rights.note: Rights in the composition are split by settlement and litigation: under the 1967 settlement James “Sugar Boy” Crawford made no claim to authorship or ownership of “Iko Iko” and was credited 25 per cent for US public performances, a share his estate and publisher hold; The Dixie Cups’ authorship of “Iko Iko” and its publisher were affirmed by a 2002 jury verdict. This page states authorship and recording history — who wrote the song and who recorded it first — and does not reproduce any lyrics. listen.what: the 1953 Checker 787 recording of “Jock-A-Mo” by Sugar Boy and his Cane Cutters — the original, not the Dixie Cups version.
listen.source: Internet Archive’s Great 78 Project: a preservation transfer of the physical Checker 787 78rpm disc, digitised by George Blood, L.P. and catalogued to the correct label, catalogue number, performer and composer credit. Because it is a scan of the 1953 object itself rather than a channel upload, it cannot be a later re-recording; its 2:34 running time is the raw disc transfer, against the roughly 2:27 recording length MusicBrainz lists for the same Checker 787 A-side.

listenCover.what: The Dixie Cups’ 1965 Red Bird single — the hand-clap and drumsticks-on-an-ashtray take that turned a 1953 New Orleans record into a standard.
listenCover.source: Auto-generated upload on “The Dixie Cups - Topic”: “Provided to YouTube by The Orchard Enterprises”, ℗ 2006 Charly Records, credited to Rosa Lee Hawkins, Barbara Ann Hawkins, Joan Marie Johnson and James Crawford. Runtime 123s (2:03), an exact match to the MusicBrainz recording dated 1964 (2:03); the rest of the MusicBrainz cluster runs 1:59-2:05, all the same master trimmed differently. Two caveats stated plainly: the ℗ line is the 2006 reissue date, not a 1964 sound-recording date, so provenance rests on Charly’s Red Bird licensing rather than an original-label credit; and I rejected the alternative UMG upload (37txS2FEVSA, 126s) because it sits on a 2023 budget compilation that credits “Producer: Sun Record Co.”, which is wrong for a Red Bird recording.
